screens.heading: Habits that protect you

teacher.say: You have learned how attacks work. Now let us build the habits that stop them.

body: Good security is mostly small habits repeated until they become automatic.

points.label: Verify independently
points.text: Check unusual requests through a phone number, address or website you already know, never through details in the message.

points.label: Use a password manager
points.text: It creates a unique password for every account, and it refuses to fill logins on lookalike addresses.

points.label: Never reuse passwords
points.text: If one site is breached or one password is phished, a unique password stops the damage from spreading.

points.label: Keep software updated
points.text: Updates close the holes that malicious files and pages try to exploit.

points.label: Reach sites yourself
points.text: Use bookmarks or type addresses for banks, email and work systems.

screens.key_takeaway: Unique passwords, independent checks and updates remove most of the risk.

screens.heading: Multi-factor authentication

teacher.say: A second step at sign-in turns a stolen password into a much smaller problem.

body: Multi-factor authentication asks for something besides your password, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get in.

points.label: Know plus have
points.text: Your password is something you know. The second factor is something you have, such as an app on your phone or a physical key.

points.label: Not all second steps are equal
points.text: Codes sent by SMS are better than nothing. Authenticator apps are stronger. Security keys and passkeys are the strongest, because they only work on the genuine website.

points.label: Never share a code
points.text: A one-time code is for you alone. Genuine support staff never need it.

points.label: Beware approval fatigue
points.text: If you receive sign-in prompts you did not start, deny them all and change your password. Attackers send repeated prompts hoping you will approve one.

screens.key_takeaway: Turn on multi-factor authentication, and never give a code to anyone.

screens.heading: I clicked. Now what?

teacher.say: Everyone slips eventually. Let us practise the response, so it is automatic when it matters.

body: Everyone clicks the wrong thing at some point. What matters is how quickly and honestly you respond. Work through the simulator and choose the best action at each step.

simulator.scenario: You clicked a link in an email and typed your work password into a sign-in page. The page then simply reloaded, and now you suspect it was fake.

options.text: Close the tab and hope nothing happens
options.feedback: Hoping is not a plan. The attacker may already be using the password, so every minute counts.

options.text: Open the real site yourself, from a bookmark, and change the password at once
options.feedback: Correct. Changing the password straight away, on the real site, takes the stolen one out of play.

options.text: Wait until Monday to mention it
options.feedback: Waiting gives the attacker time. Act immediately, even outside working hours.

steps.prompt: You used the same password on a few other accounts. What now?

options.text: Change it on every account that used it, starting with email and banking
options.feedback: Correct. Attackers try stolen passwords on other sites straight away, and email comes first because it can reset everything else.

options.text: Only the one account is at risk, so leave the rest
options.feedback: Reused passwords are tried everywhere. Every account that shares the password is at risk.

options.text: Add a 1 to the end of the old password on each account
options.feedback: Small variations are easy to guess. Use a new, unique password for each account.

steps.prompt: Your account has two-step verification. What should you do?

options.text: Turn it off, because it did not stop this
options.feedback: It did its job by adding a barrier. Turning it off removes your best protection.

options.text: Approve any pending prompts so the account stays unlocked
options.feedback: Never approve prompts you did not start. They may be the attacker trying to sign in.

options.text: Keep it on, and sign out of all other sessions from the account's security page
options.feedback: Correct. Signing out other sessions removes anyone who is already logged in with the stolen password.

options.text: Nobody, because nothing was visibly stolen
options.feedback: Damage is often invisible at first. Staying silent helps only the attacker.

options.text: Your IT or security team, immediately, with the original email
options.feedback: Correct. Reporting lets the team block the fake site, check your account and warn colleagues who got the same message.

options.text: Nobody. Delete the email so there is no evidence
options.feedback: The email is evidence that helps investigators. Report it instead of deleting it.

steps.prompt: What should you watch for over the next few days?

options.text: Nothing, because you are safe once the password is changed
options.feedback: Attackers may have set up hidden access. Stay alert for a while.
Look at your accounts, not just one bill. Signs of misuse show up in several places.

options.text: Unexpected sign-in alerts, password-reset emails, odd mailbox rules or forwarding, and unfamiliar transactions
options.feedback: Correct. These are the usual signs that someone still has access or is trying to get it.

screens.key_takeaway: After a mistake, speed and honesty matter more than perfection.

screens.heading: Reporting and what happens next

teacher.say: Reporting is not confessing. It is the single most helpful thing you can do.

body: Report quickly, even if you are unsure. Security teams would much rather receive ten false alarms than miss one real attack.

points.label: What to report
points.text: Suspicious emails, texts, calls and websites, whether or not you clicked.

points.label: What to include
points.text: Forward the original email using your organisation's report button or address, and note what you clicked or typed, and when.

points.label: If money moved
points.text: Contact your bank immediately. Fast action gives the best chance of stopping or recalling a payment.

points.label: If it was a personal account
points.text: Use the provider's account recovery and security pages, and change reused passwords everywhere.

example.title: A good outcome
example.text: A clerk realises she typed her password into a fake page. She changes it within minutes and reports it. The security team blocks the fake site and warns everyone. The attack stops with one report.

screens.key_takeaway: Report fast and without shame. A quick report turns one mistake into protection for everyone.
